chapters.title: Advanced forms
chapters.subtitle: Custom fields, dynamic formsets and validation architecture
chapters.summary: The forms layer when the basic Form is not enough: custom widgets, dynamic fields, model formsets, JavaScript-driven formsets and a validation design that stays testable.
chapters.quick_answer: Keep validation in fields, validators and `clean()`; keep widgets presentation-only. Use `modelformset_factory`/`inlineformset_factory` for repeated rows, and always render the management form. For dynamic formsets, update `TOTAL_FORMS`/`INITIAL_FORMS` with JavaScript and validate the result server-side.

sections.title: Custom fields and widgets
sections.body:
A field owns validation and conversion; a widget owns HTML. Subclass `forms.Widget` when you need a new control, and provide `template_name` plus `get_context()`/`format_value()`. Prefer `attrs` and a CSS class over a custom widget for styling.

A custom field can reuse a widget while adding `to_python()`/`validate()`. Keep the widget free of business rules.
sections.note: A widget template receives `widget`, `attrs` and `value`. Keep it a dumb renderer.

sections.title: Model formsets and inline formsets
sections.body:
`modelformset_factory` edits many rows of one model. `inlineformset_factory` edits children of one parent and sets the foreign key for you. Use `extra=0` for existing data, `can_delete=True` when removal is allowed, and `min_num`/`validate_min` for a required set.

`formset.save()` saves changed instances and deletes marked ones. Use `save(commit=False)` when you need to set fields first, then call `save_m2m()` if needed.
sections.code:
from django.forms import inlineformset_factory

OrderItemFormSet = inlineformset_factory(
    Order,
    OrderItem,
    fields=["product", "quantity"],
    extra=0,
    can_delete=True,
    min_num=1,
    validate_min=True,
)

def edit_order(request, pk):
    order = get_object_or_404(Order, pk=pk)
    formset = OrderItemFormSet(request.POST or None, instance=order)
    if request.method == "POST" and formset.is_valid():
        formset.save()
        return redirect(order)
    return render(request, "orders/edit.html", {"order": order, "formset": formset})
sections.note: An inline formset filters choices to the parent only if you pass `instance`; it does not automatically scope a `ModelChoiceField` to the tenant. Do that in `__init__`.

sections.title: Dynamic formsets and JavaScript
sections.body:
The management form tells Django how many forms were submitted. When JavaScript adds a row, clone the empty form from `formset.empty_form`, replace `__prefix__`, and increment `TOTAL_FORMS`. When removing a row, either mark `DELETE` or decrement the count and remove the node.

Never trust the client count. The server validates each submitted form and the management form; a tampered count is rejected.
sections.note: Use a stable prefix. If you render two formsets on one page, give each a different `prefix`.

sections.title: Validation architecture
sections.body:
Use three layers deliberately:

- **Field validators** for reusable, single-value rules.
- **`clean_<field>()`** for form-specific rules that need other data.
- **`clean()`** for cross-field rules, and `Model.clean()` for invariants that must hold outside forms.

Do not duplicate the same rule in all three. A validator can be shared by forms and models; a form-specific rule stays in the form.
sections.note: `add_error()` removes the field from `cleaned_data`. Read other fields with `.get()` in `clean()`.

sections.title: Forms that do not query per field
sections.body:
A `ModelChoiceField` evaluates its queryset when rendered. A form with 50 category fields can run 50 queries. Use `select_related`/`prefetch_related` on the queryset, or a single `ModelChoiceField` with a filtered queryset.

For large choice lists, use an autocomplete widget backed by an endpoint instead of rendering thousands of `<option>` elements.
sections.note: Measure with `assertNumQueries` in a form/view test. The template is part of the query count.

pitfalls: Putting business validation in a widget.
Rendering a formset without `management_form`.
Trusting `TOTAL_FORMS` from the client.
Using `extra=10` on a large existing table.
Forgetting to scope `ModelChoiceField` querysets to the current tenant/user.
Duplicating validation in forms and models with subtly different rules.
checklist: Widgets are presentation-only; fields validate.
Formsets render the management form.
Dynamic formset JavaScript updates the management count.
ModelChoiceField querysets are scoped and efficient.
Validation rules live in one obvious layer.

chapters.title: Advanced views
chapters.subtitle: CBV MRO, mixins, streaming and custom errors
chapters.summary: What is actually happening inside a class-based view, how mixins compose, and when a streaming response beats rendering a giant string.
chapters.quick_answer: A CBV is a callable object whose `dispatch()` chooses `get()`/`post()`. Mixins must come before the base view in the MRO and call `super()`. Use `StreamingHttpResponse`/`FileResponse` for large payloads; keep view logic small and move domain rules into services.

sections.title: MRO and mixins
sections.body:
Python resolves methods left to right. `class PostUpdate(LoginRequiredMixin, UpdateView)` puts the mixin first, so its `dispatch()` runs before `UpdateView.dispatch()`. If you reverse the order, the login check may never run.

A mixin should call `super()` and add one concern. If a mixin needs three unrelated hooks, it is probably a service or middleware.
sections.note: MRO is not magic: read the class from left to right and check which method calls `super()`.

sections.title: The generic-view hooks that matter
sections.body:
`get_queryset()` controls the rows; `get_object()` fetches one; `get_context_data()` adds template data; `form_valid()` handles a successful form; `get_success_url()` chooses where to go. Override the smallest hook and call `super()`.

A `ListView` paginates with `paginate_by`; a `DetailView` uses `pk`/`slug` from the URL. The generic view is a convenience, not a requirement.
sections.note: Scoping `get_queryset()` to the current user turns another user's object into a 404, which is often safer than a 403.

sections.title: Decorators on functions and methods
sections.body:
Function views take decorators directly. Class-based views need `method_decorator` on `dispatch()` or on a specific method. Stack order matters: authentication before permission, and both before side effects.

For reusable view behaviour, a mixin is usually clearer than decorating every method.
sections.note: `@method_decorator` on `dispatch` wraps every method. Apply it to `get`/`post` when only one method needs the rule.

sections.title: Streaming and file responses
sections.body:
`StreamingHttpResponse` sends an iterator of bytes; `FileResponse` streams a file and sets headers. Both avoid loading a large payload into memory. A generator that queries per chunk can still be slow; batch the queries.

For CSV exports, yield rows and set `Content-Disposition`. For private files, check permission before opening the file and never expose the storage path.
sections.note: Streaming responses cannot set a status code after the first byte. Do permission checks and validation before returning the response.

sections.title: Custom 404 and 500 pages
sections.body:
Django uses `handler404`, `handler500`, `handler403` and `handler400` from the root URLconf. The templates are `404.html`, `500.html`, `403.html` and `400.html` in the project templates directory.

With `DEBUG=False`, a 500 page hides the traceback. Log the exception and return a useful, branded page. Do not leak internal IDs or settings.
sections.note: Custom handlers are only used when `DEBUG=False`. Test them with `override_settings(DEBUG=False)`.

pitfalls: Putting a mixin after the base view in the MRO.
Overriding `dispatch()` without calling `super()`.
Loading a 2 GB CSV into a Python list before responding.
Streaming after a permission check that can still fail mid-iteration.
Relying on custom error templates while `DEBUG=True`.
checklist: Mixins are ordered correctly and call `super()`.
Querysets are scoped in `get_queryset()`.
Large exports stream and batch queries.
Private files are permission-checked before opening.
Error handlers are tested with `DEBUG=False`.

chapters.title: Advanced templates
chapters.subtitle: Custom tags, context processors, Jinja and loader performance
chapters.summary: Extend the template language without turning templates into Python: custom tags and filters, context processors, Jinja2 and the loader settings that affect every render.
chapters.quick_answer: Use `@register.simple_tag` for a value, `@register.inclusion_tag` for a fragment, and `@register.filter` for a single value transformation. Context processors add data to every template; keep them cheap. Add Jinja2 only when its syntax or ecosystem is worth a second engine.

sections.title: Custom tags and filters
sections.body:
A template tag lives in `<app>/templatetags/<name>.py`. `simple_tag` returns a value; `inclusion_tag` renders a small template; `filter` transforms one value. Tags can take `context=True` when they genuinely need the render context.

Return plain data, not HTML built by string concatenation. If you need markup, render a template and mark it safe deliberately.
sections.note: A template tag is still presentation code. Keep queries out of it or pass a prefetched object.

sections.title: Context processors
sections.body:
A context processor returns a dict merged into every template context. It runs for every render, including errors and includes. Use it for cheap, truly global data: site name, feature flags, navigation counts.

Do not run a query per request in a context processor unless you cache it. A context processor that raises takes down every page.
sections.note: The request context processor is already available; do not add a second copy.

sections.title: Jinja2 as a second engine
sections.body:
Django can run Django Templates and Jinja2 side by side. Jinja is faster for some workloads and has a richer expression language, but it is not a drop-in replacement: template tags, filters and some admin templates are Django-specific.

Use Jinja for a new surface where its syntax helps, or for a performance-sensitive template. Do not migrate a working Django-template codebase for novelty.
sections.note: Jinja templates do not see Django's `{% csrf_token %}` tag. Pass the token or use a small adapter.

sections.title: Loader and fragment performance
sections.body:
The cached template loader is enabled by default when `DEBUG=False`. In development, templates are reloaded on every change. Do not disable the cached loader in production to “fix” stale templates; deploy correctly.

`{% cache %}` caches a fragment, not a whole response. Use it for expensive, user-independent fragments and include the user/tenant in the key when the fragment is personalised.
sections.note: `{% cache %}` uses the configured cache. A fragment cached before a write can serve stale data; invalidate by key or keep the timeout short.

pitfalls: Doing database queries inside a `simple_tag` used in a loop.
Adding a context processor with a query on every request.
Marking template-tag output safe without escaping.
Assuming Jinja supports every Django template tag.
Caching a personalised fragment without the user in the key.
checklist: Custom tags return data or render a template, not hand-built HTML.
Context processors are cheap and exception-safe.
Jinja is used deliberately, not as a default.
Cached fragments include user/tenant keys when needed.
Templates are tested with the real context.

chapters.title: Advanced URL routing
chapters.subtitle: Custom converters, resolve(), i18n patterns and error handlers
chapters.summary: URLconf beyond path(): custom converters, reverse/resolve introspection, namespaced includes and locale-prefixed routes.
chapters.quick_answer: Register a converter class with `register_converter()` when a route needs a domain type. Use `reverse()` to build URLs and `resolve()` to inspect the matched route. Namespaces keep apps isolated. Add `i18n_patterns()` only when public URLs should carry a language prefix.

sections.title: Custom path converters
sections.body:
A converter has a regex, `to_python()` and `to_url()`. Register it once, then use `<name:value>` in routes. `to_url()` must produce a string that the regex matches.

Converters are a good place for domain identifiers: order numbers, tenant slugs, date segments. They are not authorization checks; the view still scopes the object.
sections.note: A converter that accepts too much pushes validation into the view. Keep the regex precise.

sections.title: reverse() and resolve()
sections.body:
`reverse()` turns a route name plus arguments into a URL. `resolve()` turns a path into a `ResolverMatch` with `view_name`, `kwargs`, `url_name` and `app_name`. `request.resolver_match` is the match for the current request.

Use `resolve()` for breadcrumbs, analytics or middleware that needs the view name. Cache the result if it is called on every request.
sections.code:
from django.urls import resolve, reverse

url = reverse("blog:detail", kwargs={"slug": "django-forms"})
match = resolve("/blog/django-forms/")
match.view_name      # "blog:detail"
match.kwargs         # {"slug": "django-forms"}
match.app_name       # "blog"

request.resolver_match.url_name  # in a view or middleware
sections.note: `reverse()` raises `NoReverseMatch`; do not catch it broadly. A missing route is a bug, not a user error.

sections.title: Namespaces and included URLconfs
sections.body:
`include((patterns, app_name), namespace=...)` lets two instances of the same app coexist with different namespaces. This is common for multi-tenant or white-label sites.

With a namespace, `reverse("shop:detail")` includes it. A missing `app_name` is the usual reason a namespaced reverse fails.
sections.code:
# config/urls.py
urlpatterns = [
    path("shop/", include(("shop.urls", "shop"), namespace="shop")),
    path("admin-shop/", include(("shop.urls", "shop_admin"), namespace="shop_admin")),
]

# shop/urls.py
app_name = "shop"
urlpatterns = [path("<slug:slug>/", views.detail, name="detail")]

reverse("shop:detail", kwargs={"slug": "lamp"})
reverse("shop_admin:detail", kwargs={"slug": "lamp"})
sections.note: Two namespaces can share the same view functions. The namespace is part of the route identity.

sections.title: Locale-prefixed URLs
sections.body:
`i18n_patterns()` wraps routes with a language prefix and activates the language from the URL. Keep language-independent routes (health, API, webhooks) outside the prefix.

Set `LANGUAGE_CODE`, `LANGUAGES` and `LocaleMiddleware`. Use `{% get_current_language %}` and `{% language %}` in templates. Do not prefix API endpoints unless clients expect it.
sections.code:
from django.conf.urls.i18n import i18n_patterns
from django.urls import include, path

urlpatterns = [
    path("health/", health),
    path("api/", include("api.urls")),
]

urlpatterns += i18n_patterns(
    path("", include("pages.urls")),
    prefix_default_language=False,
)
sections.note: With `prefix_default_language=False`, the default language has no prefix and the other languages do. Test both shapes.

sections.title: Trailing slashes, APPEND_SLASH and handlers
sections.body:
`CommonMiddleware` redirects `/blog` to `/blog/` when `APPEND_SLASH=True` and the slashless route does not match. This only works for GET/HEAD; a POST to a slashless URL will lose its body on redirect. Generate canonical URLs with `{% url %}` instead of relying on the redirect.

Custom error handlers live in the root URLconf and are used only when `DEBUG=False`.
sections.note: A redirect from a POST is a bug. Always include the trailing slash in forms and links.

pitfalls: Using a broad converter regex and validating in the view.
Catching `NoReverseMatch` and returning a 200 page.
Forgetting `app_name` for a namespaced include.
Putting webhooks behind `i18n_patterns()`.
Relying on `APPEND_SLASH` for POST requests.
checklist: Custom converters are precise and tested.
Every route has a name and namespace.
`reverse()` is used for internal links.
Locale prefixes cover only public pages.
Error handlers are tested with `DEBUG=False`.
